text:
California Catholic Conference urges support for teen social media ban bill
LAX Leader
The California Catholic Conference is urging residents to contact lawmakers in support of AB 1709, a proposed bill that would prohibit social media companies from offering "addictive features" to children under 16 years old, according to an Aug. 26 action alert.
In its alert, the organization cited several studies indicating that social media can be harmful to young children. The alert stated, "Since 2007, rates of depression, anxiety, and self-harm have skyrocketed, especially among teen girls. The average teen spends nearly five hours a day on social media. Young people self-report feeling addicted, experiencing damaging messages to their body image and self-esteem from the comparisons and endless scrolling, receiving unwanted contact by strangers, and exposure to harmful content including eating disorders, suicidal ideation, violence, pornography, and drug use." The statement continued: "Children have the right to be children and to parental protection from harmful materials. Establishing the age of receiving a social media account at 16 helps preserve children's social and emotional development and parents' rights to safeguard their children from such harms."
The CCC's call comes as parents and leaders around the world address concerns about smartphones' effects on young people. In December 2025, Australia banned social media for all individuals under 16 years old; this has prompted other countries and U.S. states to propose similar legislation.
On Aug. 26, Meta Platforms agreed to pay $17 billion in settlement over a lawsuit concerning teen social-media addiction.
In Los Angeles over the past two years, the Unified School District limited screen time for students and banned all students from bringing or using smartphones while on campus.
A July Pew survey found that 56% of Americans supported some form of ban on social media use for those aged 16 or younger.
